title: Quad Foreign Ministers Will Meet in the Philippines This Month. A Trump Visit to India May Follow.
excerpt: US Ambassador Sergio Gor confirmed the Manila meeting on the sidelines of ASEAN and revealed plans for a Quad leaders' summit — potentially bringing President Trump back to India.
body:
The Quad is accelerating. US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor confirmed on Tuesday that the foreign ministers of all four Quad nations — the United States, India, Japan, and Australia — will convene in the Philippines within the next two to three weeks, marking the second ministerial gathering in barely two months.

The meeting will take place on the sidelines of the 59th ASEAN Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Manila, scheduled for July 20-22. It comes just weeks after the 11th Quad Foreign Ministers' Meeting was held in New Delhi in May, where the four partners announced new initiatives on maritime security, critical minerals, and supply chain resilience.

## Beyond Manila

What made Gor's announcement at the USISPF Leadership Summit particularly notable was what he said next: the Philippines meeting would not replace other planned Quad engagements but would be followed by a ministerial meeting in Australia — and, ultimately, by a Quad leaders' summit.

"We do aim to have a Quad meeting at some point, a ministerial Quad meeting in Australia," Gor told the audience. "And followed ultimately by a leaders' meeting which we're trying to nail down. That would include President Trump coming to India."

A Trump visit to India would carry enormous symbolic weight. The President's last visit — in February 2020, when he was greeted by more than 100,000 people at the Motera Stadium in Ahmedabad — remains one of the most talked-about diplomatic spectacles of his first term. Gor noted that Trump "holds it in a very fond place" and "continues to talk about it."

## What's on the Agenda

The Manila meeting is expected to build on the framework established at the New Delhi ministerial. Key areas of focus include:

**Maritime security**: The Quad has been deepening naval cooperation across the Indo-Pacific, with a particular focus on the Indian Ocean and South China Sea. The New Delhi meeting announced the expansion of the Indo-Pacific Logistics Network and a new framework for joint maritime domain awareness.

**Critical minerals**: The Quad Critical Minerals Initiative, launched to diversify supply chains away from Chinese dominance, has moved from framework to implementation. The Philippines, rich in nickel and copper, is a natural partner for this effort.

**Economic resilience**: With the US-Iran ceasefire still fragile and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz only partially restored, energy security remains a pressing concern for all four Quad partners. India, which imports nearly 90 per cent of its crude oil, has a particular stake in ensuring open sea lanes.

**China**: Though the Quad carefully avoids naming China directly, the grouping's entire architecture is oriented around maintaining a "free and open Indo-Pacific" in the face of Beijing's growing assertiveness. The choice of the Philippines — which has been at the sharp end of Chinese maritime pressure in the South China Sea — as the venue sends its own signal.

## An Alliance That's Speeding Up

The pace of Quad engagement has visibly quickened since Trump's return to office. The May meeting in New Delhi produced concrete deliverables: a new Ports of the Future Partnership, enhanced information-sharing on maritime threats, and commitments on undersea cable security. The announcement of a Manila meeting barely seven weeks later suggests the four partners are moving toward a standing rhythm of quarterly ministerial contact.

For India, the Quad serves a dual purpose: it anchors New Delhi's role as a major Indo-Pacific power while providing a multilateral frame for the increasingly deep bilateral relationship with the United States. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar has described the Quad as "a platform for practical cooperation" rather than a military alliance — a framing that gives India the strategic flexibility it values.

## Why NRIs Should Care

The Quad's trajectory directly affects the security and economic environment that shapes diaspora life. Stronger Indo-Pacific partnerships mean more stable supply chains for businesses with US-India exposure, more robust defence ties that underpin the broader relationship, and a diplomatic architecture that treats India as a co-equal partner rather than a junior ally.

A potential Trump visit to India for a Quad leaders' summit would be a major diplomatic event — and a powerful signal to the nearly five million Indian Americans that the world's two largest democracies are building something durable.

*Sources: USISPF, Devdiscourse, Bharat Horizon, ANI, ASEAN Secretariat*
